title: Peacekeeping and Monitoring in Nagorno-Karabakh
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: After the war in Nagorno-Karabakh ended, a ceasefire agreement was signed on ten November 2020. Russia sent a peacekeeping group to the region to watch the ceasefire between Armenian and Azerbaijani forces. This group had nearly two thousand soldiers led by Lieutenant General Rustam Muradov. They set up posts along the contact line and near Stepanakert.
pages.caption: The opening of the Russian-Turkish Joint Monitoring Centre.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Российско-турецкий центр по контролю за перемирием открылся в Азербайджане 04.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The opening of the Russian-Turkish Joint Monitoring Centre.

pages.text: The Russian peacekeepers started helping the Red Cross to find and exchange fallen soldiers. Later, they also began demining the region to make it safer. Turkey and Russia agreed to create a joint monitoring center. Turkey sent sappers and officers to help with demining and training. The monitoring center opened at the end of January 2021.
pages.caption: Overview of border disputes and clashes from December 2020 to April 2021

evidence.articleCaption: Overview of border disputes and clashes from December 2020 to April 2021

pages.text: However, the region faced many challenges and ceasefire violations. Clashes happened near some villages in the Hadrut Province. These villages became a holdout during the fighting. The Russian peacekeeping contingent briefly took control of one village before it came under Azerbaijani control. Both sides accused each other of restarting the conflict.
pages.caption: Russian peacekeepers and Azerbaijani military personnel near Dadivank of Kalbajar District.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Russian peacekeepers and Azerbaijani military personnel near Vank village.png
evidence.articleCaption: Russian peacekeepers and Azerbaijani military personnel near Dadivank of Kalbajar District.

pages.text: Over time, more incidents caused worry and international criticism. In late 2021, a civilian was killed during farm work by shelling. In 2022, armed forces entered the territory and set up an observation post, leading to drone strikes and casualties. Russia publicly assigned blame to Azerbaijan for violating the agreement. Later, Azerbaijani forces withdrew from one village.

In March 2023, during an ongoing blockade, Azerbaijani forces crossed the line of contact again. They occupied a strategic height and brought engineering equipment. The Russian peacekeepers asked them to stop and withdraw. Meanwhile, Azerbaijan stated their forces took control measures to stop the transport of military means on dirt roads.

Following the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War, a trilateral ceasefire agreement was signed on 10 November 2020. In accordance with this accord, Russia deployed a peacekeeping contingent consisting of nearly two thousand servicemen to the region. Led by Lieutenant General Rustam Muradov and headquartered near Stepanakert, these forces established observation posts along the contact line and the Lachin corridor to monitor the ceasefire between Armenian and Azerbaijani forces.
pages.caption: The opening of the Russian-Turkish Joint Monitoring Centre.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Российско-турецкий центр по контролю за перемирием открылся в Азербайджане 04.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The opening of the Russian-Turkish Joint Monitoring Centre.

pages.text: Alongside the Russian mission, Turkey and Russia established a joint monitoring center near Marzili in Azerbaijan. Turkish sappers and officers arrived to assist with demining operations and train local personnel. The monitoring center officially opened on 30 January 2021, utilizing unmanned aerial vehicles and personnel from both nations to monitor ceasefire compliance under the guard of Azerbaijani soldiers.
pages.caption: Overview of border disputes and clashes from December 2020 to April 2021

evidence.articleCaption: Overview of border disputes and clashes from December 2020 to April 2021

pages.text: Despite the presence of peacekeepers, significant violations occurred. Clashes erupted near Hadrut around an Artsakh holdout pocket comprising specific villages and a monastery. After initial confusion and brief Russian control, the villages ultimately came under Azerbaijani control, with both sides trading blame for the renewed violence.
pages.caption: Russian peacekeepers and Azerbaijani military personnel near Dadivank of Kalbajar District.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Russian peacekeepers and Azerbaijani military personnel near Vank village.png
evidence.articleCaption: Russian peacekeepers and Azerbaijani military personnel near Dadivank of Kalbajar District.

pages.text: Tensions persisted through subsequent years. In October 2021, a local civilian was killed by cross-border shelling during agricultural work, prompting investigations and mutual accusations. In March 2022, Azerbaijani forces entered the territory, resulting in drone strikes and casualties. For the first time, the Russian Ministry of Defence publicly blamed Azerbaijan for violating the ceasefire agreement, though disputes over subsequent troop withdrawals remained.

By March 2023, amidst a prolonged blockade, peacekeepers reported that Azerbaijani forces had crossed the line of contact, occupied a strategic height, and set up engineering equipment. Russia requested a withdrawal to previous positions, while Azerbaijan maintained that its actions were necessary to suppress military transportation along northern dirt roads.

In the aftermath of the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War, peacekeeping operations were initiated by Russia in the region to monitor the ceasefire between Armenian and Azerbaijani forces. Russia sent a peacekeeping contingent of 1,960 servicemen led by Lieutenant General Rustam Muradov. Additionally, Turkey and Russia established a joint monitoring centre in Azerbaijan.
pages.caption: The opening of the Russian-Turkish Joint Monitoring Centre.

pages.text: Initial humanitarian mandates included assisting the International Committee of the Red Cross with the exchange of fallen soldiers and initiating comprehensive demining operations. However, the mission immediately encountered geopolitical friction. Azerbaijani authorities criticized the peacekeepers for exhibiting a perceived pro-Armenian bias, pointing to leadership engagements with local officials and the contested use of administrative terminology, which strained the intended neutrality of the deployment.

pages.text: The fragility of the cessation of hostilities was underscored by localized military engagements. Armed clashes materialized around an Artsakh holdout pocket in the Hadrut Province. Despite initial Russian intervention, disputed territorial demarcations resulted in specific villages falling under Azerbaijani control amid reciprocal accusations of ceasefire violations.

pages.text: Subsequent years witnessed recurrent kinetic incidents and escalating humanitarian crises. In October 2021, fatal shelling during agricultural work triggered diplomatic recriminations regarding targeted displacement. A more acute escalation occurred in March 2022 when Azerbaijani units crossed the line of contact, precipitating drone strikes and casualties. Notably, this prompted Russia to publicly attribute ceasefire violations directly to Azerbaijan, diverging from prior diplomatic ambiguities.

By March 2023, during an ongoing blockade that drew international censure, peacekeepers documented further territorial advancements by Azerbaijani forces across the line of contact. While Russian command formally requested a withdrawal of national armed forces to prior positions, Azerbaijan defended its deployment as a localized measure to interdict military supply routes, highlighting the persistent limitations of the peacekeeping architecture.

title: History and Impact of Student Activism
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Student activism is work by young people to cause political, environmental, economic, or social change. Student groups often play big roles in democratization and winning civil rights. Modern movements span all ages, races, and political views.
pages.caption: City University of Hong Kong students staging a sit-in during 2014 Hong Kong protests over blocking of electoral reforms

evidence.articleCaption: City University of Hong Kong students staging a sit-in during 2014 Hong Kong protests over blocking of electoral reforms

pages.text: In Argentina, student protests grew into a major political force after 1900. In 1918, students started the University Revolution in Córdoba. This movement wanted to make education institutions much more democratic.
pages.caption: Shimer College students protesting threatened changes to the school's democratic governance, 2010

evidence.articleCaption: Shimer College students protesting threatened changes to the school's democratic governance, 2010

pages.text: In Chile, students led nationwide protests from 2011 to 2013. They demanded a new framework for education, including more state participation and an end to profit in higher education.
pages.caption: Students raise the flag of Argentina at the University of Córdoba, 1918.

evidence.articleCaption: Students raise the flag of Argentina at the University of Córdoba, 1918.

pages.text: During communist rule, students in Eastern Europe were behind several famous protests. Peaceful student demonstrations in Budapest started the events that led to the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. In Czechoslovakia, Jan Palach set fire to himself in 1969 to protest against the Soviet-led occupation.
pages.caption: Students protest against Bill 78 in Montreal, 2012.

evidence.articleCaption: Students protest against Bill 78 in Montreal, 2012.

pages.text: In Ireland, pro-Palestinian protesters set up tents in Fellows Square in May 2024. These protests were led by the student union from Trinity College Dublin to call for divestment.

B1-B2.headline: History and Impact of Student Activism

pages.text: Student activism involves efforts by students to drive political, environmental, economic, or social change. Beyond education, student groups frequently help secure civil rights and advance democratization across diverse global contexts.
pages.caption: City University of Hong Kong students staging a sit-in during 2014 Hong Kong protests over blocking of electoral reforms

evidence.articleCaption: City University of Hong Kong students staging a sit-in during 2014 Hong Kong protests over blocking of electoral reforms

pages.text: Student movements span varied backgrounds and political perspectives. While some protests focus on internal institutional affairs like disinvestment, others target broader global issues, wars, or authoritarian regimes. Modern student activism is most often associated with left-wing politics across many countries.
pages.caption: Shimer College students protesting threatened changes to the school's democratic governance, 2010

pages.text: In Argentina, student activism became a major political force after 1900. The 1918 University Revolution in Córdoba triggered a general modernization of universities to increase democratic participation. The Córdoba Manifesto encapsulates the interests of students during this time to make their institutions more democratic.
pages.caption: Students raise the flag of Argentina at the University of Córdoba, 1918.

evidence.articleCaption: Students raise the flag of Argentina at the University of Córdoba, 1918.

pages.text: Between 2011 and 2013, Chile experienced massive student-led protests demanding a new educational framework, greater state participation, and the elimination of profit from higher education. These demonstrations reflected a deep discontent with Chile's high level of inequality, involving both peaceful marches and violent clashes.
pages.caption: Students protest against Bill 78 in Montreal, 2012.

evidence.articleCaption: Students protest against Bill 78 in Montreal, 2012.

pages.text: In Eastern Europe, students challenged communist rule through prominent protests. Peaceful student demonstrations in Budapest famously sparked the chain of events leading to the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. In Czechoslovakia, student Jan Palach committed suicide by setting fire to himself to protest the Soviet-led occupation.

In May 2024, Trinity College Dublin student union led a pro-Palestinian encampment in Fellows Square. After a five-day protest, during which the Book of Kells exhibition was blocked, the college pledged to divest from Israeli companies following similar actions elsewhere.

Campus activism encompasses concerted efforts by student constituencies to instigate political, environmental, economic, or social transformation. Historically, these groups have frequently catalyzed democratization and the securing of civil rights alongside their standard educational pursuits.

title: The Evolution of the Bicycle
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Long ago, people invented a new way to travel on two wheels. The first vehicle of this kind did not have pedals. A German inventor named Karl von Drais made it. People called it the dandy horse or draisienne. The rider sat on a wooden frame and pushed the machine with their feet while steering the front wheel.
pages.caption: 1886 Swift Safety Bicycle

evidence.fileTitle: File:1886 Swift Safety Bicycle Coventry Transport Museum.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: 1886 Swift Safety Bicycle

pages.text: In the early years, inventors tried different ideas. Some claims about early two-wheeled vehicles are disputed. Later in France, inventors added a mechanical crank drive with pedals on a larger front wheel. This machine was mass-produced. People also called it a boneshaker because it had a rigid frame and iron-banded wheels that caused a rough ride.
pages.caption: Wooden draisine (around 1820), the earliest two-wheeler

evidence.fileTitle: File:Draisine or Laufmaschine, around 1820. Archetype of the Bicycle. Pic 01.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Wooden draisine (around 1820), the earliest two-wheeler

pages.text: To go faster, makers built high-wheel bicycles with a very large front wheel and a smaller rear wheel. These bicycles were difficult to mount and brake. Because they were dangerous, riding them was mostly for adventurous young men. Victorian fashion and high seats made these machines hard for many people to use safely.
pages.caption: Drais's 1817 design made to measure

evidence.articleCaption: Drais's 1817 design made to measure

pages.text: Later, inventors created the safety bicycle. It used a chain drive connected to the rear wheel instead of pedals on the front wheel. This design had a lower seat and a double-triangle diamond frame. These changes made riding much safer and easier for both men and women of different ages.
pages.caption: A couple seated on an 1886 Coventry Rotary Quadracycle for two

evidence.articleCaption: A couple seated on an 1886 Coventry Rotary Quadracycle for two

pages.text: More improvements followed to make riding comfortable. Inventors introduced the practical pneumatic tire, which soon became very popular. Other new parts included the rear freewheel, derailleur gears, and hand-operated brakes. Cycling remained very important in Europe, while use in the United States dropped as automobiles became the preferred choice.

The history of the bicycle began with the invention of the dandy horse, also known as the draisienne or running machine. Created by German Baron Karl von Drais, it was the first human transport to use two wheels in tandem without pedals. Riders sat astride a wooden frame and pushed themselves along with their feet while steering the front wheel.
pages.caption: 1886 Swift Safety Bicycle

evidence.fileTitle: File:1886 Swift Safety Bicycle Coventry Transport Museum.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: 1886 Swift Safety Bicycle

pages.text: During the 1860s in France, bicycle design advanced significantly when inventors added pedals and a mechanical crank drive to an enlarged front wheel. This machine entered mass production and became widely known as the boneshaker due to its rigid iron-banded wheels and frame. Although it allowed riders to travel faster than before, its fixed design and high front wheel created noticeable stability and comfort issues.
pages.caption: Wooden draisine (around 1820), the earliest two-wheeler

evidence.fileTitle: File:Draisine or Laufmaschine, around 1820. Archetype of the Bicycle. Pic 01.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Wooden draisine (around 1820), the earliest two-wheeler

pages.text: To achieve greater speeds, manufacturers developed the high-wheel bicycle featuring a massive front wheel and a tiny rear wheel. However, these machines were dangerous, difficult to mount, and hard to brake. Because falls were common and high seats posed risks, cycling with these ordinary bicycles remained largely restricted to adventurous young men rather than risk-averse individuals or women constrained by contemporary fashion.
pages.caption: Drais's 1817 design made to measure

evidence.articleCaption: Drais's 1817 design made to measure

pages.text: The introduction of the safety bicycle transformed the industry. By utilizing a chain drive that connected frame-mounted cranks to the rear wheel, inventors solved the problem of simultaneous pedaling and steering. Lower seat heights and the eventual adoption of the double-triangle diamond frame made cycling accessible to a much broader public, shifting public perception from a dangerous sport to everyday transport.
pages.caption: A couple seated on an 1886 Coventry Rotary Quadracycle for two

evidence.articleCaption: A couple seated on an 1886 Coventry Rotary Quadracycle for two

pages.text: Further technological progress sparked a second bicycle craze during the 1890s. The invention of the practical pneumatic tire greatly improved comfort, while rear freewheels, coaster brakes, and derailleur gears added new levels of control. While cycling continued to flourish throughout Europe for commuting and racing, its popularity declined dramatically in the United States during the early twentieth century as automobiles gained dominance.

The foundational predecessor of the modern bicycle was the dandy horse, or draisienne, engineered by German Baron Karl von Drais. Established as the earliest human-powered transport utilizing two in-line wheels, it lacked any pedal mechanism. Propulsion relied entirely on the rider straddling a wooden frame and pushing against the ground with their feet while manually directing the front steering assembly.
pages.caption: 1886 Swift Safety Bicycle

evidence.fileTitle: File:1886 Swift Safety Bicycle Coventry Transport Museum.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: 1886 Swift Safety Bicycle

pages.text: Subsequent developmental phases during the 1860s witnessed French inventors integrating rotary cranks and pedals directly onto the hub of an enlarged front wheel. This commercially successful mass-produced vehicle, colloquially termed the boneshaker, utilized metal and wood construction to reduce weight. Nevertheless, the inherent rotational speed limitations and rigid frame geometry generated severe ride discomfort and stability challenges for operators.
pages.caption: Wooden draisine (around 1820), the earliest two-wheeler

evidence.fileTitle: File:Draisine or Laufmaschine, around 1820. Archetype of the Bicycle. Pic 01.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Wooden draisine (around 1820), the earliest two-wheeler

pages.text: The logical progression of the boneshaker manifested in the high-wheel bicycle, where front wheel enlargement permitted enhanced velocity constrained primarily by the rider's leg length. Despite innovations such as wire-spoke tension wheels, these vehicles remained hazardous and difficult to mount, braking efficiently was problematic, and their operational risks largely restricted their use to adventurous demographics rather than cautious riders or women bound by contemporary attire.
pages.caption: Drais's 1817 design made to measure

evidence.articleCaption: Drais's 1817 design made to measure

pages.text: A pivotal paradigm shift occurred with the advent of the safety bicycle. By employing a chain drive that linked frame-mounted cranks to the rear wheel, designers successfully decoupled propulsion from steering. Subsequent incorporation of lower seating configurations and the double-triangle diamond frame redefined bicycles as practical utility transport for men and women across diverse age groups.

evidence.articleCaption: A couple seated on an 1886 Coventry Rotary Quadracycle for two

pages.text: The 1890s Golden Age of Bicycles was catalyzed by technological refinements that elevated comfort and mechanical efficiency. The introduction of practical pneumatic tires eliminated much of the traditional roughness, while auxiliary developments like rear freewheels, hand-operated cable brakes, and early derailleur mechanisms expanded operational control. Geographically, while European cycling maintained cultural and economic prominence through commuting and racing, American adoption suffered a dramatic decline as motorized automobiles ascended to transport dominance.

pages.text: Further technological progress sparked a second bicycle craze during the 1890s. The invention of the practical pneumatic tire greatly improved comfort, while rear freewheels, coaster brakes, and derailleur gears added new levels of control. While cycling continued to flourish throughout Europe for commuting and racing, its popularity declined dramatically in the United States during the early twentieth century as automobiles gained dominance.

title: Tracing the History of Diabetes
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The medical condition known today as diabetes has a very long history. People talked about it in Ancient Egypt and ancient India. Long ago, doctors noticed that patients produced a lot of urine. Later, physicians in India also found that the urine tasted sweet and named it honey urine.
pages.caption: Frederick Banting (right) joined by Charles Best in office, 1924

pages.text: In ancient China, the condition was called wasting-thirst. Traditional doctors described symptoms and treatments in old books. Later, people began using a modern term that means sugar urine disease. This new term may have come from ancient exchanges with Ayurvedic doctors in India.

pages.text: Greco-Roman accounts mostly talked about passing too much water. Roman writers described how the amount of urine was greater than the fluid a person drank. Some early medical texts also mentioned that patients felt very thirsty and tired all the time.

pages.text: During the Islamic Golden Age, physicians preserved and studied ancient medical knowledge. Over many centuries, European doctors also shared new ideas. Thomas Willis suggested in 1674 that diabetes could be a disease of the blood rather than just the kidneys.

pages.text: In the late nineteenth century, researchers discovered the role of the pancreas. Scientists later found insulin and used it to help patients. In the early 1920s, a team in Toronto purified insulin for medical use, changing treatments forever.

The history of diabetes spans thousands of years across multiple ancient civilizations. The earliest possible reference appears in the Ebers Papyrus from Ancient Egypt, which mentions eliminating plentiful urine. However, historians note it remains unclear if this specifically described diabetes or urinary infections.

pages.text: In the fifth and sixth centuries BC, Ayurvedic physicians in India observed the sweet taste of diabetic urine, naming the condition madhumeha or honey urine. Meanwhile, traditional Chinese medicine described and treated the illness as wasting-thirst, a term documented in classical medical literature over many centuries.

Authors like Aulus Cornelius Celsus described an imbalance where excreted fluid exceeded fluid intake. Islamic physicians later synthesized these global medical traditions during the Islamic Golden Age, laying crucial foundations for later European advances.

pages.text: Understanding shifted gradually as anatomical knowledge improved. In 1674, Thomas Willis proposed that diabetes might originate in the blood rather than just the kidneys. Later, Johann Peter Frank distinguished diabetes mellitus from diabetes insipidus in 1794, separating conditions that share excessive urination symptoms.

pages.text: The formal discovery of the pancreas in diabetes occurred in 1889 through Joseph von Mering and Oskar Minkowski. Following early twentieth-century hypotheses about an internal secretion called insulin, researchers including Frederick Banting and Charles Best successfully purified insulin in Toronto, transforming patient care.

The conceptual evolution of diabetes involves a complex interplay of ancient medical traditions. The Ebers Papyrus from Ancient Egypt contains a potential early reference to polyuria, though scholars debate whether the terminology denotes diabetic symptoms or urinary tract infections. In ancient India, Ayurvedic physicians identified sweet urine, introducing the designation madhumeha.

pages.text: Parallel developments occurred in traditional Chinese medicine, where the condition was characterized as wasting-thirst. Historical monographs from the Sui and Tang dynasties expanded these diagnoses, with Zeng Liyan noting glycosuria and Wang Tao compiling detailed case reports containing descriptions of sweet urine.

pages.text: Classical Greco-Roman literature emphasized excessive fluid excretion without recording urinary sweetness. Celsus documented an imbalance between ingested and excreted volumes, while Byzantine compilers like Oribasius categorized the condition as a renal disorder. These fragmented insights were later synthesized by scholars in the medieval Islamic world.

pages.text: Pathophysiological understanding advanced as anatomical investigation progressed through autopsy. Thomas Willis hypothesized a hematological origin in 1674, challenging renal assumptions. By 1794, Johann Peter Frank formally delineated diabetes mellitus from diabetes insipidus, while nineteenth-century French clinicians distinguished clinical phenotypes comparable to ancient Ayurvedic classifications.

pages.text: The twentieth century marked a therapeutic turning point. Following the identification of the islets of Langerhans and hypotheses regarding carbohydrate-regulating secretions, researchers isolated and purified insulin. The subsequent assignment of the insulin patent to the University of Toronto for a symbolic dollar ensured widespread clinical accessibility.
